column2: How does nomination process work in academy awards?
column3:
he Oscar nomination process is essentially a multi-stage filtering and voting process, and the key thing is that different Academy branches nominate in different categories.

For the current Academy rules, it works roughly like this:

Films first have to be eligible. A film must satisfy the Academy’s release, theatrical exhibition, submission, and category-specific requirements. Eligible films are placed on the Academy’s official reminder lists.
Some categories have a preliminary/shortlist round. Before nominations, categories such as Documentary Feature, International Feature, Visual Effects, Original Song, Original Score, Makeup and Hairstyling, Sound, and several shorts are narrowed to a shortlist. The exact procedure differs by category.

Academy members vote for nominees. Most nominations are chosen by members of the relevant professional branch. In simple terms:

Actors nominate actors
Directors nominate directors
Writers nominate writers
Costume designers nominate costume designers, etc.

This is one of the most important features of Oscar nominations.

Best Picture is different. Eligible members across all 19 Academy branches may nominate films for Best Picture. Under the current rules, voters rank up to 10 films in order of preference, and the 10 highest-performing films become the nominees.
Some other categories are also exceptions. For categories such as International Feature and some animated/short-film categories, eligible members across multiple branches can participate if they meet the category's viewing requirements. So the rule "each branch nominates its own profession" is a useful simplification, but it isn't universal.
The votes are secret and independently counted. Oscar ballots are submitted electronically and tabulated by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), not by Academy executives deciding who should be nominated.

After nominations are announced, there is a separate final voting round. At that stage, all eligible Academy members can vote across all 24 categories, subject to viewing requirements. Beginning with the 98th Oscars, members must have watched all nominated films in a category to vote in that category.

A simplified picture is:

Eligible films → possible shortlist → branch nomination voting → nominees announced → all-member final voting → Oscar winners

For Best Actor specifically, the process is therefore roughly:

Eligible acting performances → Actors Branch votes → top nomination results become the five nominees → entire eligible Academy votes among those nominees → winner.

One interesting current change: beginning with the 99th Oscars, an actor can be nominated for more than one performance in the same acting category if multiple performances independently finish in the top five. Previously, that was restricted.

This also explains why predicting nominations from box office results or critic scores isn't straightforward: the nomination electorate is often a specialized subset of Academy members, while the winner is selected by a much broader electorate.

column2: Compare countries by their life expectancy vs. population. Is there a correlation?
column3:
The important limitation is that the dates do not line up exactly: the life-expectancy article ends at 2010–2015, while the population article provides populations for 2022 and 2023. So this is a cross-country comparison of population size versus relatively recent historical life expectancy, not a same-year analysis. The two source articles are the country life-expectancy list and the UN-based population list.

After normalizing country names and matching the two tables, I was able to compare 182 countries. Using 2023 population and 2010–2015 life expectancy, the result is striking:

Correlation measure        Result        Interpretation
Pearson: population vs. life expectancy        0.001        Essentially no linear correlation
Pearson: log(population) vs. life expectancy        −0.079        Extremely weak negative relationship
Spearman rank correlation        −0.072        Essentially no monotonic relationship

A Pearson correlation of 0.001 is almost exactly zero. In other words, based on these two articles, a country's population size tells us essentially nothing about its life expectancy.

Some examples make that easier to see:

Country        Population, 2023        Life expectancy, 2010–15
India        1.438 billion        67.57
China        1.423 billion        75.67
United States        343.5 million        78.88
Indonesia        281.2 million        68.60
Pakistan        247.5 million        65.86
Nigeria        227.9 million        51.88
Japan        124.4 million        83.28
Switzerland        8.9 million        82.69
Iceland        0.39 million        82.19

Notice what happens among the large countries. India and China have almost the same population size, yet their reported life expectancies differ by about 8 years. Nigeria is also one of the world's largest countries by population but has a life expectancy of only 51.88 years, while Japan is much smaller and has the highest value in the matched dataset at 83.28 years.

The reverse is true among high-life-expectancy countries: they vary enormously in population.

High-life-expectancy country        Population        Life expectancy
Japan        124.4M        83.28
Switzerland        8.9M        82.69
Spain        47.9M        82.52
Italy        59.5M        82.35
Singapore        5.8M        82.34
Australia        26.5M        82.30
Iceland        0.39M        82.19

So countries with approximately 82–83 years of life expectancy range from fewer than 400,000 people to more than 124 million people.

Conclusion

There is no meaningful correlation between country population size and life expectancy in these two datasets.

The numerical result is particularly strong:

Population → Life expectancy: r ≈ 0.00

That doesn't mean life expectancy has no relationships with other country characteristics. It only means that population size itself does not appear to explain life expectancy based on these articles.

There is also a useful RAG/reasoning aspect to this question: the answer cannot simply be retrieved from either article. A system has to retrieve two separate tables, identify compatible country entities, deal with mismatched naming, choose comparable columns, join the datasets, and then calculate an aggregate statistic that appears in neither source. That's a substantially different problem from factual retrieval

column2: For winter olympics, list events that were added in the last 100 years in order they were added listing the year they were added.
column3:
If by “events” you mean Winter Olympic sports/disciplines that were newly added to the medal program, here is the chronological sequence over roughly the last 100 years. I’m treating an event as “added” when it first became an official medal discipline, rather than counting every new distance, weight class, or mixed-team event.

Year added        Sport / discipline
1936        Alpine skiing
1960        Biathlon
1964        Luge
1992        Freestyle skiing
1992        Short-track speed skating
1998        Snowboarding
1998        Curling (returned as an official medal sport)
2002        Skeleton (returned to the Olympic program)
2026        Ski mountaineering

There are two important caveats. Curling and skeleton aren't truly “new” in 1998/2002: curling was an official medal sport at the first Winter Games in 1924, while skeleton appeared in 1928 and 1948 before later returning. The IOC therefore describes curling as being added back to the program in 1998, and ski mountaineering as the newest actual sport, debuting in 2026

column2: Which olympics, Russia did not participate in?
column3:
Russia or the Soviet Union as an official national Olympic team, there are several important cases:

Olympics        What happened
Los Angeles 1984 Summer Olympics        The Soviet Union did not participate. It withdrew/boycotted the Games along with most Soviet-bloc countries. This is the clearest case of complete non-participation.
PyeongChang 2018 Winter Olympics        Russia was officially banned, but approved Russian athletes competed as Olympic Athletes from Russia (OAR). So Russian athletes participated, but not under the Russian flag/team name.
Tokyo 2020 Summer Olympics (held 2021)        Russia did not compete under its national name because of doping sanctions. Russian athletes competed as the ROC (Russian Olympic Committee) team.
Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics        Again, athletes competed as ROC, not as Russia. The IOC documentation explicitly refers to competitors as representing the Russian Olympic Committee.
Paris 2024 Summer Olympics        Russia did not enter an official national team. A limited number of eligible Russian athletes could compete individually as Individual Neutral Athletes (AIN), without Russian national symbols.
